BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: A weak low pressure system will move east of the area on Wednesday, resulting in breezy afternoon winds but no precipitation.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Rain and high elevation snow decreasing from west to east today.
- Cooler with gusty winds today and tonight. Near to slightly above normal temperatures through the week.
- Dry Monday through Wednesday, then a slight chance of precipitation late week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: An area of low pressure will move east across the area today. Showers will continue this morning across southwest Idaho, tapering off from west to east this afternoon before ending in the Magic Valley this evening. An additional 0.25 to 0.50 inch of rain is expected across south-central Idaho, including the Magic Valley. Rain amounts will taper off to less than 0.10 inch for the Boise Metro area and west-central Idaho mountains, with minimal amounts across southeast Oregon. Snow levels will remain around 6500-8000 feet, limiting additional light snow accumulations to the peaks.

A weak cold front accompanying the low will also move across the area. This will bring slightly cooler temperatures, with highs decreasing by about 5 degrees from yesterday. The surface pressure gradient will tighten behind the front starting this afternoon and increasing tonight, supporting northwest wind gusts of 20-35 mph. The strongest winds will be along a corridor from Baker City southeast to the Snake River Plain, with gusts 35-45 mph between Mountain Home and Twin Falls. Despite the rain today, gusty winds tonight will prevent widespread fog formation, although patchy fog will still develop in sheltered mountain valleys and across portions of southeast Oregon.

Winds will decrease on Monday as a ridge of high pressure builds overhead. Higher elevations will see slight warming while valleys experience similar temperatures. On Tuesday, winds will become breezy from the southeast as a low pressure system approaches the area from the west, strongest east of Boise where gusts will reach 20-30 mph. Temperatures will warm a few more degrees, especially the lower elevations where breezy conditions will aid mixing. Clouds will increase as the system approaches but it will remain dry.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A weak low pressure system will move east of the area on Wednesday, resulting in breezy afternoon winds but no precipitation. Additional systems will move by to the north on Thursday and Friday, resulting in a 10-30% chance of showers on Thursday and a 20-40% chance on Friday, highest across the north. An upper level ridge will build back in over the weekend with dry conditions returning. The weak systems Wednesday through Friday will bring slight cooling, but temperatures will still be near normal. Slightly warmer temperatures will arrive over the weekend as the ridge builds in.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Once this system moves through, northwest flow aloft looks to hold for Thursday and Friday keeping highs in the upper 50s to low 60s for the plains. Another cold front is possible as we get to the weekend with unsettled weather looking to return as well.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Areas of fog again through Sunday morning across portions of northeast and eastern Colorado.
- Unsettled weather returns today and persists through early Tuesday.Mountain snow is likely (>70% chance) above 8500ft during thistime, with a few inches of snow expected.
- Scattered rain showers and cooler temperatures for the plains on Monday. A few snowflakes possible for the Palmer Divide on Monday night.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Current satellite imagery shows some mid-level clouds as well as some patchy fog in Morgan County, eastern Elbert County, and northern Lincoln County. Areas of dense fog or low stratus look possible once again through this morning for northern Colorado and along/near the Palmer Divide. This fog could make it as far south as the northern Denver metro and east to DIA. Still some questions about how widespread and/or dense the fog will be...A Dense Fog Advisory may be needed later this morning if confidence increases through the overnight. Otherwise, lows tonight will stay in the 40s in the plains and 20s and 30s for the high country.

Sunday will be another nice afternoon with high temperatures in the 60s for the plains, but there will be more clouds compared to Saturday. Some wind gusts of 20-30 mph are possible in the afternoon mainly across the eastern plains. Southwest flow aloft through at least Monday midday continues to bring rich moisture to our area. The trough to our west looks to move rather quickly from the Great Basin on Sunday afternoon to eastern Colorado by Monday evening. A low looks to form in southeast Colorado on Monday evening, but the strongest energy continues moving off to the northeast. At the surface, a cold front is progged to move through early on Monday morning and make it through our southeast counties by Monday afternoon. Therefore, temperatures on Monday afternoon do not look to warm up very much from the low 50s and possible even falling into the upper 40s on the plains. Have nudged Monday afternoon temperatures down based on the latest short-term guidance. Monday afternoon also looks windy for most of the plains with some gusts of 30-40 mph and isolated wind gusts up to 50 mph. Only slightly lower wind gusts are still possible through Tuesday for the eastern plains.

In terms of precipitation: Light rain/snow showers should move into the high country on Sunday afternoon with widely scattered light rain showers by the evening for the plains given the unfavorable southwest flow aloft initially. Snow levels look to start rather high on Sunday afternoon (> 12,000 ft) and then quickly drop by Sunday evening into the overnight to around 10,000 feet. We expect a further decrease in snow levels to 8,500 to 9,000 feet by Monday afternoon. Therefore, snow becomes increasingly likely above about 8,500 to 9,000 ft for late Sunday, through Monday, and lingering into early Tuesday morning. The northern mountains look most favored for the higher snowfall amounts in our area. Given the current snowfall forecasts and limited scope of the heaviest totals, we have held off on issuing a Winter Weather Advisory. One may be needed in a future forecast package. The north flow behind the front introduces an upslope component for the Palmer Divide where QPF could be maximized on Monday evening. As we get into Monday night and early Tuesday morning, colder air continues to filter in, so snow levels could drop low enough (down to about 7,000-7,500 ft) for a few flakes on the Palmer Divide. No snow accumulation is expected there given the decreasing precipitation chances. Overall, we have slightly increased QPF from the previous forecast for the next 48-60 hours for locations in the high country and Palmer Divide.

Some ridging moves in for Tuesday with temperatures rebounding into the upper 50s to low 60s for the plains. Another trough moves through on Wednesday with another round of precipitation possible though the signal for this remains murky. Some snow looks possible again for the high country with rain showers possibly spilling onto the plains once again. At this time, have low PoPs for this potential starting Wednesday evening.

Once this system moves through, northwest flow aloft looks to hold for Thursday and Friday keeping highs in the upper 50s to low 60s for the plains. Another cold front is possible as we get to the weekend with unsettled weather looking to return as well.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Mid-week and beyond, ridging will try to build back in over the region, but a few moisture starved upper level lows will hamper a potential warming trend. Overall, temperatures are expected to remain fairly close to seasonal averages during this period.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - The latest round of localized fog is expected to gradually
- A complex but disorganized storm system will move into the area Sunday, bringing multiple rounds of rain and snow showers through Tuesday AM.
- Expect widespread rain in Carbon county today with scattered showers developing elsewhere.
- After a late afternoon lull, look for another round of scattered showers plus isolated thunderstorms Sunday evening into early Monday morning.
- Additional showers are expected to fill in during the day and evening Monday, with snow mixing in above about 5000 ft.
- Widespread windy conditions are anticipated Monday and Monday night.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: TODAY: The weather pattern will turn more active today through Monday night as a complex storm system approaches the area. GOES satellite imagery shows abundant mid to upper level cloud cover streaming into the area this morning as deep moisture is pulled into the area once again. In addition, we have yet another round of patchy fog across much of the area this morning, but it is not quite as widespread as the last few days. Expect fog to increase through daybreak, and gradually dissipate by early afternoon. Looking ahead to the primary storm system, our two main players we have been watching for several days are entering the scene this morning. The first is the primary elongated upper level trough now pushing into the northern California, while the second is a moisture-laden upper level low riding the sub-tropical jet into the southwestern CONUS this morning. Mid to upper level moisture is expected to surge into the area today, pushing precipitable water values to around 0.75" in Wyoming and possibly over 1" in western Nebraska. These values are absurdly high for early November, and more reminiscent of a late summer monsoon surge. In fact, NAEFS mean PW exceeds the climatological maximum over much of the area. While atmospheric moisture is clearly abundant, the question as always is if we can get this moisture to the ground. Short range model guidance shows a region of positive theta-e advection pushing in from the southwest around daybreak, first into Carbon county and then spreading northeastward through mid afternoon. This round will be generally in the form of scattered showers, though the Sierra Madre range and southwest Carbon county should see more consistent rainfall with favorable southwest orographic ascent. Snow levels will be extremely high for this time of year when precipitation starts today. Rain is expected to fall at least at 10 kft, if not even 11 kft, meaning that we could see rain up to ridge-top in the Sierra Madre. With cloudy skies expected all day, temperatures were nudged downward towards high resolution model guidance, but we should still reach the mid 50s for all valley areas. Forcing for ascent should weaken a bit mid afternoon as a weak leading vort-max passes through, decreasing coverage slightly, but expect to see some shower activity around the area for most of the day today.

TONIGHT: By this evening, the mid-level low pressure system is expected to be centered around western Wyoming. As the primary trough axis approaches, we should see ascent increase again after sunset, this time encompassing more areas east of the Laramie range too. RAP guidance depicts decent overrunning lift combined with frontogenesis as the surface lee cyclone begins to take over in northeastern Colorado this evening. In addition, there is potential for considerable elevated instability over the Nebraska panhandle this evening. Thus, expect to see shower coverage increase after about 7-8PM, with isolated thunderstorms anticipated as well. Due the extremely abundant moisture, locally heavy rainfall will be possible with this round this evening through very early Monday morning. The primary trough axis and surface cold front are expected to clear the area by about 5AM Monday, ending the warm phase of the storm system.

MONDAY: At sunrise Monday, most precipitation should be confined to the fringes of the forecast area, generally in Carbon, Converse, and Niobrara counties. By this time, a powerful surface cyclone will be strengthening and moving northeastward, pulling in a tight pressure gradient on its western flank (over our area). At the same time, we should see moisture and marginal isentropic ascent wrapping back into the area on the back-side as the mid-level low closes off. Expect winds to rapidly increase Monday morning with precipitation gradually spreading to the south and east of its daybreak position as the day progresses. Forcing aloft is marginal and there is some bust potential for this last round of precipitation to fail to materialize. In order to get widespread rainfall to fill in (and get more appreciable amounts) we will want to see a secondary mid-level low pressure center over southern Colorado elongate the primary system and turn winds in the 750 to 500-mb layer from northwest (which is where they are expected to be Monday morning) to north or northeast. This scenario is depicted by the HRRR, while the RRFS keeps winds aloft just west of north, and thus ends up considerably drier across the entire area Monday into Monday evening. The official forecast favors the ECMWF ensemble mean, which is somewhere in between the high resolution models on each extreme. The most likely scenario fills light to moderate precipitation in to the southeast through the day on Monday and into the evening hours. Strong surface northwest flow will allow some terrain features to stand out, particularly the sub-ridges of the High Plains. The most favorable area for notable moisture in the wrap-around phase is the US-20 corridor from Douglas to Chadron, with a secondary favored area possible along the southern Laramie range and the north side of the Cheyenne ridge (Laramie to Chugwater to Chugwater. Areas where northwest flow is downsloping (Wheatland to Scottsbluff and Cheyenne to Kimball) look a little more marginal, and we will likely need stronger lift aloft to overcome the surface downslope flow.

SNOW POTENTIAL: As colder air is pulled into the system on Monday, expect snow levels to drop quickly. Accumulating snow should begin in the Sierra Madre and Snowy ranges early Monday morning. By mid- morning, we should see some snow mixing into the lower elevations of Carbon county and around the I-80 summit (once precipitation fills back in there). During the afternoon and evening hours, we should see snow levels continue to drop, allowing some flakes to fly as low as about 5000 ft. It is important to note that with systems like this, the precise snow level will probably depend somewhat on the precipitation rates, with heavier rates flipping over to snow and lighter rates remaining as rain. Confidence is increasing in accumulating snow in the mountains, with probabilities for advisory criteria amounts around 70 to 90% in the Snowy, northern Laramie, and Sierra Madre ranges. The higher elevations of I-80 (Arlington/Elk Mountain and the I-80 summit) are sitting around 60% chance for advisory criteria snow accumulation. All of the above locations currently have about a 30% chance for warning criteria amounts. Outside of those zones, confidence decreases considerably, as which lifting scenario (see previous paragraph) will strongly impact snow potential outside of the higher elevations too. Of the populated areas, Laramie is most likely to see accumulating snow (80% chance), followed by Rawlins and Saratoga (60% chance). These probabilities decrease east of the Laramie Range, but Douglas, Lusk, and Cheyenne all have about a 10-30% chance to see accumulating snow, mainly late Monday afternoon and evening. Snow is not expected to stick (if it flies at all) below about 5000 ft.

WIND POTENTIAL: Monday will be quite windy across much of the area as a strong surface pressure gradient develops over the Plains. The wind direction is not really aligned with most of our typical gap wind areas, and the lack of synoptic descent (or even synoptic ascent) along with the unusual wind direction aloft (due north) decreases confidence. While some high resolution models (e.g. HRRR) are very aggressive on the surface wind gusts, the other factors are keeping confidence too low to issue any High Wind Watches at this time. It will absolutely be windy, with high confidence in gusts 45 to 55 mph, but it looks quite marginal to exceed the critical 58 mph threshold in most areas. For the wind prone areas, the I-80 summit and the I-25 corridor between Wheatland and Glendo look to be the most favorable zones, with around a 40% chance for high winds. Over the Plains, the most likely areas to exceed criteria will be where northwest flow is downsloping (e.g. south sides of the Pine and Cheyenne ridges). Probabilities remain around 30 to 40% for Cheyenne, Kimball, Sidney, and Alliance.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Drier air will move in Tuesday morning, bringing an end to precipitation, though the end time has slightly slowed compared to previous forecasts. While not nearly as strong as Monday, breezy to windy northwest winds are expected to continue into Tuesday with highs rebounding to near seasonal averages. Look for plentiful sunshine to return to the area Tuesday as well.

Mid-week and beyond, ridging will try to build back in over the region, but a few moisture starved upper level lows will hamper a potential warming trend. Overall, temperatures are expected to remain fairly close to seasonal averages during this period. Conditions look generally dry too, though a compact upper level low passing through Wednesday may bring a few rain and/or high elevation snow showers. Expect winds to be light Wednesday through Friday, but a few ensemble members show stronger winds moving into the area with an upper level low passing north of us over the weekend.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Behind this system, conditions dry out for a few days as high amplitude ridging moves overhead. We'll see a slight warm up through the mid-week period, although highs remain 5-10 degrees below normal for early November.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - The Flood Watch continues for southeast Utah and southwest Colorado as an atmospheric river brings rain, rainshowers, and snowfall to the area.
- Several rivers across southwest Colorado are forecast to reach minor flooding stage.
- The San Juan River at Pagosa Springs is forecast to reach major flood stage which has prompted a Particularly Dangerous Situation Flood Warning for that area.
- Winter weather highlights have been issued for the San Juans and central Colorado mountains for accumulating snow Sunday morning through Monday evening.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A weak shortwave moved across the area today with only a few showers and storms noted on radar. A few showers remain across the area at this hour but are trending downwards and this will continue. Good news for the trick or treaters this evening. Satellite is showing plenty of cloud cover to our southwest, poised to move into the area very shortly.

More widespread precipitation will begin falling between midnight and 3am thanks to a potent Atmospheric River (AR). This AR remains forecast to bring anomalous precip to our CWA for the next 24 to 36 hours. PWATs from the ensemble GFS and EC remain in the 250 - 350% range for this time of year, no change there. Widespread rain and rainshowers, possibly some embedded thunderstorms, will bring valley rainfall to near/at an inch for the central valleys, and 2 to 2.5 inches for the Four Corners valleys eastward, less up north. 1.5 to 2.5 is likely for the Book Cliffs/Tavaputs and central mountains while the San Juans may see 3 to 4 inches of liquid precip. The Flood Watch remains in effect for southeast Utah and southwest Colorado as already saturated soils, along with this rainfall, may result in flash flooding and debris flow issues, not to mention river flooding. Rivers are expected to respond quickly to this additional rainfall, especially in the Pagosa Springs area.

As far as snow is concerned, snow levels will remain above 10K feet, if not a bit higher, before dropping Sunday afternoon onwards. Amounts remain in the 12 to 18 inch range with locally higher amounts still possible so the Winter Storm Warning remains in effect. The Advisories also remain in effect for the central mountains, Grand Mesa, and Flat Tops where 5 to 10 inches are expected. As snow levels lower late Sunday night into Monday morning, some of this snow will reach pass level. Be prepared for sloppy driving conditions during the Monday morning commute along US-550, US-50, and along I-70 over Vail Pass.

Behind this system, conditions dry out for a few days as high amplitude ridging moves overhead. We'll see a slight warm up through the mid-week period, although highs remain 5-10 degrees below normal for early November. Looking further out, a quick moving clipper system has the potential to bring some light showers to the region mid-to-late next week, although model agreement is poor.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Tuesday - Saturday: For the remainder of the forecast period, active weather can be expected for south central and southeastern Colorado.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Significant and dangerous flooding is expected to start today across portions of the San Juan Mountains and adjacent San Luis Valley.
- Heavy and wet snow is expected across the San Juan Mountains late tonight into tomorrow morning.
- Unsettled pattern continues through the week, with additional disturbances passing over.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Today - Tomorrow Night: Through Sunday and Monday, dangerous and high impact flooding is expected across the San Juan Mountains, as another round of heavy precipitation impacts the region.

Synopsis: A dynamic pattern will take place today through Monday across south central and southeastern Colorado. The subtropical jet will be pushing northward, as a digging trough advances southeastward/eastward on the north side of the subtropical jet. This will bring a prolonged period of forcing and moisture into the region. With the forcing and moisture in place, widespread precipitation is expected, with the heaviest and most impactful moisture across the San Juan Mountains. In addition, as the storm pattern pushes eastward, strong winds are expected both today and tomorrow, with the strongest winds on Monday across the plains. Given various complex hazards, this discussion has been broken down into the main concerns with this storm system.

Precipitation/Flooding San Juan Mountains: As this storm system impacts the area, widespread precipitation is anticipated, with the heaviest and most prolonged showers across the already soaked San Juan Mountains. This is going to lead to a significant flooding event across the San Juan Mountains and adjacent San Luis Valley. Examining the latest data, there has been a concerning trend with this storm systems evolution, primarily that of the subtropical jet pushing further north and slowing the forward progression of the trough. What this ultimately means is that colder air with the trough will be slower to get into the region, which means snow levels will be higher to start, and slower to fall heading into Monday morning. This all comes together to mean more rain and more rain-on-snow melting, and overall less snow. In addition, another concerning trend within the latest guidance is an increase in QPF, with many high-res models and ensembles strongly supporting 4-6 inches of liquid, and potentially locally higher amounts. The latest forecast will reflect this trend. All of this will greatly increase the flooding potential and risk, and several rivers are expected to rise into Moderate to Major flood stages starting this evening and through Monday, with some rivers even expected to set new record crest levels. There is a realistic possibility that current river forecast are too conservative with how high they take the flooding. Along with that, road washouts will be possible and mudslides/rockslides can be expected. To those in the San Juan Mountains and the adjacent San Luis Valley, please heed any evacuation warnings and road closures, and please do not drive through flood waters... remember, Turn Around, Don't Drown... doing these things could save your life. Finally, once the trough does start to push over, and cooler air filters in, snow levels are expected to lower. Overall, about 8-14 inches of heavy wet snow is anticipated along the San Juan Mountains. This could cause dangerous and slick travel along mountain roads, especially by late Sunday night and Monday morning, when colder air is pushing into the area.

Precipitation Elsewhere: Across the rest of the forecast area, showers can be expected, though to a lesser degree. Across the rest of the mountains, snow can also be expected, with the greatest snow again late Sunday night and into Monday as the colder air with troughing filters in. Most other ranges can expect to see around 4- 10 inches of heavy wet snow. This snow may still cause pockets of slushy and slick roads, so extra caution should still be given across the rest of the higher terrain when it's snowing. For the valleys and plains, rain showers will dominate, with no snow anticipated. Coverage for showers across these areas will be greatest Sunday for the valleys, and then Monday for the plains as the storm system pushes eastward and a cold front drops southward, bringing additional surface forcing. Along with that, a band of highly forced convective thundershowers along the leading eastern edge of the troughing/subtropical jet interface will be possible across the eastern plains late Sunday evening. These showers may bring pockets of gusty winds around 45-50 mph and occasional rumbles of thunder.

With all of that said, any precipitation across the area late Monday is expected to start decreasing in coverage and intensity, as the broader storm system continues to push eastward, and both forcing and moisture lessen.

Wind: Along with the precipitation, this pattern will bring strong winds to the region both today and tomorrow, though in different fashions. Throughout Sunday, strong southerly to southwesterly winds can be expected ahead of the storm system. Winds will be greatest across the mountains and San Luis Valley simply given closer proximity to the stronger flow aloft, and then across the far eastern plains, where the surface gradient will tighten in response to lee troughing development. Winds in these regions will be sustained around 20-35 mph, with gusts up to around 50 mph. Then heading through Sunday afternoon into Monday morning, strong winds are expected to continue, though primarily across the southern Sangre de Cristo Mountains and the northeastern portions of the Raton Mesa. Reverse shear, and an eventual mountain top inversion, will help to force stronger winds aloft to the surface, with pockets of 50-60 mph likely along the immediate leeward side of these features. Isolated 70 mph wind gusts can not be ruled out. Finally, heading through Monday, as the storm system pushes east, winds will become northerly to northwesterly across south central and southeastern Colorado. Strong winds will again be expected Monday, though with the strongest primarily across the eastern plains, where the gradient will tighten through the day and into the night as the trough becomes more wrapped up across the central US. Winds gusts across the region will be 30-50 mph, with the strongest of those gusts across the plains. As the storm system treks east, winds will lessen Monday night, though will remain gusty across the plains.

Other: Outside of the flooding and wind concerns, you can expect a fairly typical setup with a stormy pattern in place. Much of the area will have mostly cloudy to cloudy skies through Monday as the system passes over. Then as for temperatures, values will be warmest and above seasonal values Sunday ahead of the system, especially across the plains as downsloping takes place. Then for Monday, temperatures cool some as the system passes over and a cold front starts to push southward, with values near to slightly below seasonal values.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Tuesday - Saturday: For the remainder of the forecast period, active weather can be expected for south central and southeastern Colorado. While the Sunday-Monday storm system will be exiting the region through Tuesday, additional waves are anticipated to pass over the area through the week, which will bring brief periods of increased precipitation chances and breezier winds. Any precipitation chances will be greatest along the mountains, where forcing will be maximized. With that all said, while confidence is high (60-70%) in the unsettled pattern, uncertainty does still remain in how individual waves will evolve given the messy pattern that develops. Otherwise, mostly clear to partly cloudy skies and fairly stable, and near seasonal, temperatures can be anticipated through the week.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Mid level ridging will bring temporary dry and stable conditions late Monday through Tuesday, with a more progressive wave forecast to translate through the region Wednesday into Thursday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - There is a Moderate Risk for Excessive Rainfall (level 3 of 4) across portions of southern Utah, as a surge of moisture brings widespread rainfall across the region. A Flood Watch is in effect for much of southern and east central Utah late tonight through Sunday evening.

- Accumulating mountain snow is expected across all Utah mountains Sunday through Monday morning. Upwards of 12" of snow is expected above 9000 feet, and 3-6" of snow down to around 7000 feet. Upper elevations of the Cottonwoods and western Uintas may see localized accumulations 18-24".
- Cool, dry, and stable conditions will temporarily build in Tuesday, with another weak storm system expected during the Wendesday-Thursday timeframe.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: An inland-penetrating Atmospheric River (AR) coupled with a deep upper trough spreading into the Great Basin later tonight through Sunday will bring widespread rain and high elevation snow to the forecast area over the next 36 hours. This AR is currently making landfall with widespread precipitation quickly spreading across the lower deserts of southern CA and AZ. This moisture will quickly spread across the forecast area from south to north overnight, and persist through Sunday morning.

The forecast has remained fairly consistent over the past couple of days, with locally upwards of 3" of additional rain across orographically favored areas of southern Utah from the Pine Valleys east to Boulder Mountain, and 1+ inches of rain in lower elevations including St George, Cedar City, Zion Canyon and Kanab. Given recent rainfall over the past few weeks, antecedent conditions are nearly saturated and runoff is expected to be very efficient, resulting in another round of flooding across southern and east central Utah beginning late tonight, and continuing through Sunday.

As the region of enhanced IVT shifts east of the forecast area Sunday afternoon, the upstream trough will spread into the Great Basin, with increasing large scale ascent interacting with an already saturated airmass to maintain widespread precipitation through the afternoon and into the evening. Cooling temperatures aloft will begin lowering snow levels from west to east during the afternoon, with snow levels falling below 8000 feet by late Sunday evening across nearly the entire forecast area excluding the far southeast. As this trough progresses into the central Rockies, a favorable period of post-frontal orographics looks to persist along the I-15 corridor through Sunday night, before gradually winding down Monday morning. Total snow accumulation looks to run in the 3-6" range below 9000 feet, while higher elevations will be pushing 12"+, and perhaps upwards of 20" in the upper Cottonwoods. Low elevation rainfall totals will likely exceed 1" across most northern valleys including much of the Wasatch Front through Monday morning.

Mid level ridging will bring temporary dry and stable conditions late Monday through Tuesday, with a more progressive wave forecast to translate through the region Wednesday into Thursday. This quick-hitting wave will lack the moisture tap of recent events, thus precipitation totals will remain fairly light. Long range models lean heavily toward longwave ridging building into the region next weekend into early in the following week.

2660.travel_advice: Dangerous avalanche conditions. Careful snowpack evaluation, cautious route-finding and conservative decision-making essential.

product.author: Krista Beyer
bottom_line: A Special Avalanche Advisory is in effect for the North and South San Juan Mountains and the La Plata Mountains.

A potent winter storm increases avalanche hazard throughout the day Sunday into Monday. Rain, snow, and wind impacts will rapidly change avalanche conditions. Give large, connected slopes in the alpine a large buffer, as avalanches can release naturally, breaking wider and travelling further than expected.

2747.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes lack enough snow to produce an avalanche. If you find a steep slope with firm, continuous snow close to ridges, go around it to avoid the hazard.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe to travel on as they have very little snow. On high-elevation north-, northeast-, and east-facing slopes, if you find firm, hollow snow, you could trigger an avalanche. If in doubt, just walk around these drifts of snow.
